name: Larne
title: Thickness Measurement in Larne | Ferry and Cargo Ship UTM
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Larne Harbour: ro-pax ferries on the Cairnryan route, bulk and project cargo ships, vehicle decks, ramps, tanks, piping.
h1: Ship Thickness Gauging at Larne Harbour and Larne Lough
intro: Larne sits at the mouth of Larne Lough on the County Antrim coast, on the shortest sea crossing between Northern Ireland and Scotland. The harbour's main business is the ro-pax ferry service to Cairnryan, with dry bulk, general and project cargo ships and occasional expedition cruise calls. A ferry returning to the same berth day after day can be gauged in instalments, and a cargo ship staying a day or more in one visit. For each Larne job, technicians travel out from India and work around the timetable or the cargo plan.
keywords: project cargo ship inspection northern ireland

highlights.p: The Cairnryan ferries spend only a short time at Larne between crossings, but they do it every day. Staging vehicle-deck, ramp, bow and ballast tank readings over a run of turnarounds builds a complete picture without taking a ship off the route.

Dry bulk, general and heavy-lift ships stay alongside far longer than the ferries do. Their holds, hatch covers and crane pedestals can be gauged and crack-checked while cargo is worked, usually within a single call to the harbour.

Larne Lough shelters the berths from the North Channel. Ships at the cargo quays lie steady, and deck and tank work carries on in weather that would stop launch boarding at an anchorage outside the harbour entrance.

port.h: Larne Harbour: ferry gateway on the North Channel
p: Larne Harbour lies just inside the entrance to Larne Lough, a long, narrow inlet protected on its eastern side by the Islandmagee peninsula. The approach from the North Channel is short and direct, which is why Larne has been a ferry port for well over a century: the crossing to Loch Ryan on the Scottish coast is the shortest commercial sea route between the two islands. Unlike Belfast and Warrenpoint, both trust ports, Larne is privately owned and closely tied to the ferry business that dominates it. Ships approaching meet the strong tidal streams of the North Channel, and fog and winter gales can unsettle the timetable, but once inside the entrance the berths are well protected. The Chaine Memorial Tower beside the harbour entrance is a familiar mark for masters on the final approach.

P&O Ferries' ro-pax service to Cairnryan is the backbone of the port, carrying freight trailers, cars and passengers on a tight daily cycle. The route feeds supply chains running between Northern Ireland and the markets of Scotland and England, so the ferries are worked hard and their dockings are short and carefully slotted into the year. The harbour also handles dry bulk and general cargo, and project cargo that needs open quay space close to the sea; large components for onshore energy schemes have come in this way. Expedition and small cruise ships call from time to time, landing passengers for the Antrim coast. Across the lough, the Ballylumford power station on Islandmagee is a reminder that this shoreline has long served energy as well as trade.

The ferry pattern sets the rhythm of inspection. A Cairnryan ferry may be alongside only long enough to discharge and reload, but because it comes back to Larne several times a day, every day, a superintendent can spread readings across a fortnight of calls instead of fitting them into one. The quieter sailings, and overnight calls where the timetable allows, are the best time for tank entry, when fewer crew are tied up with loading. Cargo ships at the general quays give the opposite profile: fewer calls, but stays long enough to open holds and tanks properly. Ferry operators tend to hold refits in the quieter months of the year, so pre-refit gauging often falls in the autumn, ahead of the annual overhaul at a yard away from Larne.

At the ferry berths, the work is organised around the linkspan and the loading plan. The team boards once the ship is secured, takes vehicle-deck plating, ramp hinges and lashing points in lanes the chief officer has cleared, and then goes below to ballast tanks, voids and engine-room piping that the crew prepared on the previous crossing. MPI on ramp and bow-door hinge lugs fits naturally into the same visits. Every reading is tied to the same frame references each time, so a programme spread over many turnarounds produces one coherent report rather than a pile of fragments.

The general cargo quays offer more conventional conditions: a bulk or project ship alongside for a day or more, holds opened as cargo comes out, and the lough's shelter keeping the ship still. Larne has no drydock, so bottom shell, sea chests and propeller areas are left for the docking, which for Larne ferries and cargo ships usually means Belfast, a yard on the Mersey or a continental yard. Ships sometimes wait at anchor in the lough or off the entrance; launch work is possible there through the agent, although the anchorage outside the entrance is exposed to the North Channel and the window can close quickly.
list: Ferry berths for the Cairnryan route — vehicle-deck, ramp, bow-door and ballast tank readings staged across consecutive turnarounds.
Ferry engine rooms — sea-water, fire-main and scrubber piping UT during quiet or overnight calls.
General cargo quays — hold, hatch cover and tank gauging on dry bulk, general and project cargo ships alongside for a day or more.
Heavy-lift and project cargo calls — MPI and DPI on crane pedestals, lifting points and deck sockets between lifts.
Larne Lough and the outer anchorage — launch-borne deck readings on ships waiting for a berth, weather permitting.

context.h: Regulation and trade on the Larne–Cairnryan corridor
p: Port state control at Larne is carried out by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency within the Paris MoU. Ro-pax ships on the crossing face frequent scrutiny because they carry passengers, whatever flag they fly, and the cargo ships calling at the general quays are targeted on the usual risk profile. For older ferries, the condition of vehicle-deck plating, bow and stern door structure and ballast tanks draws the closest attention from inspectors and class surveyors, because the cycle of heavy axle loads, salt water carried aboard on vehicles and constant ramp operation wears these ships in predictable places.

A crossing from Larne to Cairnryan begins and ends in the UK, so it falls outside the EU's emissions trading system and FuelEU Maritime, which only bite on voyages touching EU ports. A ship that moves between Larne and an Irish or continental port brings those EU obligations with it for that leg. The post-Brexit trading arrangements for Northern Ireland change the customs handling of the goods on board, not the standard the ship is judged by: hull, tanks and decks are assessed against the same class rules and IACS requirements as anywhere else. For operators keeping older tonnage on the route, that makes steady, well-documented gauging between refits part of normal fleet management.

jobs.h: Thickness gauging jobs we see at Larne
jobs.p: Most Larne work is for ferry operators and is staged, with each turnaround contributing a slice of the scope. The rest comes from cargo ships on single calls, where the job has to be finished within one stay. In both cases we agree with the superintendent which areas the attending surveyor at the next docking or survey will want figures for, and order the work so that those are measured first. Short-notice requests are common after a ramp or deck incident, and MPI is often added to the gauging when that happens. Reports are issued in class TM formats, with the ferry readings consolidated into one document at the end of the programme.
list: Pre-refit gauging on a Cairnryan ro-pax ferry, spread over two weeks of turnarounds so the yard has a steel and pipe list before the annual overhaul.
Vehicle-deck and ramp inspection after reported damage, with UT for wastage and MPI on hinge lugs and ramp fittings.
Ballast tank and void space gauging on a ferry, one or two tanks per call, ahead of an intermediate survey.
Hold and hatch coaming gauging on a dry bulk ship during discharge at the general cargo quays.
Crack detection on crane pedestals and sea-fastening points on a heavy-lift ship between project cargo lifts.

logistics: Belfast International and George Best Belfast City airports are both within reach of Larne by road, and the railway from Belfast ends at Larne Harbour station beside the ferry terminal. Long-haul arrivals usually connect through London or another European hub to Belfast. The team travels from India on UK visas, applied for once the programme is agreed; for a staged ferry job we plan one visit covering a series of turnarounds rather than repeated trips. Terminal access is ISPS-controlled and arranged through the ship's agent or the ferry operator.

faqs.q: Can a Cairnryan ferry be gauged without missing a sailing?
faqs.a: Yes, if the work is staged. Each turnaround at Larne is short, so the team takes a defined slice: a section of vehicle deck, one ramp, or a ballast tank the crew opened and ventilated on the crossing over. Over consecutive calls the slices add up to the full scope. The chief officer decides what is released each time, and the team is off the car deck before loading starts.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Larne?
faqs.a: No. Ferries and cargo ships based at or trading to Larne dock at Belfast, at yards on the Mersey or on the Continent. Gauging at Larne is therefore in-service work: internal structure, decks, tanks and piping measured while the ship keeps trading, so that the docking period is spent on renewal rather than on discovering what needs renewing.

faqs.q: Which parts of a ro-pax ferry need most attention on this route?
faqs.a: On a short, high-frequency crossing the vehicle decks, ramp structure and bow or stern door arrangements take repeated heavy loading, and ballast tanks see frequent changes as trim is adjusted. Engine-room sea-water piping and, on scrubber-fitted ships, wash-water lines also wear quickly. These are the areas we suggest measuring first, with MPI on hinge lugs and ramp fittings.

faqs.q: Can you gauge project cargo ships calling at Larne?
faqs.a: Yes. Heavy-lift and project cargo ships usually stay alongside long enough to gauge holds, tween decks and hatch covers, and to crack-check crane pedestals, lifting lugs and deck sockets with MPI or DPI. We plan around the lift sequence, because some areas only become accessible once a particular piece of cargo has been landed on the quay.
